title: 3. Distribution, Supply Chain & Unit Economics

epigraph.quote: Every $100 of weighted revenue across XLP's core bellwethers converts into $9.97 of operating cash flow and $6.42 of free cash flow.
epigraph.author: XLP Core Constituent Unit Economics Audit

web_blocks.text: 3.1 Dual Distribution Architecture: Direct-to-Store (DSD) vs. Warehouse & Omnichannel

web_blocks.html: Understanding XLP's unit economics requires tracing how goods move from factory to pantry. Two distribution models dominate the fund. First, Direct-Store-Delivery (DSD) and Bottler Networks (used by PepsiCo's Frito-Lay, Coca-Cola's bottlers, and Mondelez) bypass retailer central warehouses. Route drivers stock snacks and drinks directly onto store end-caps and convenience-store coolers. DSD maximizes freshness and impulse visibility, though it carries heavy driver and fleet costs. Second, Omnichannel Store-Fulfilled & Club Warehouses (Walmart, Costco, Target) use automated regional centers, cross-docking, and store backrooms as local fulfillment hubs. In Q4 FY26, Walmart's eCommerce grew 24%, with expedited store-fulfilled delivery up over 50%.

web_blocks.text: 3.2 Weighted $100 Revenue-to-FCF Waterfall Across Core XLP Constituents

web_blocks.html: Because an ETF does not file a consolidated GAAP income statement, we must build an economic look-through waterfall from audited constituent filings. We take five audited non-tobacco bellwethers—Walmart (11.37%), Costco (9.82%), Procter & Gamble (7.90%), Target (4.34%), and PepsiCo (4.15%)—which represent 37.58% of XLP's weight. For each company, we normalize its latest full fiscal year income and cash-flow statements to a $100 revenue baseline, using matching fiscal periods throughout. We then weight those figures by their exact XLP portfolio weights.

web_blocks.caption: XLP Core Constituent Basket: Weighted $100 Revenue-to-FCF Unit Economics (WMT, COST, PG, TGT, PEP)
web_blocks.takeaway: On a weighted $100 of revenue, XLP's core retail-and-CPG basket pays $69.32 in COGS, $19.38 in OpEx ex-D&A, and $2.32 in D&A to earn $8.98 EBIT—converting into $9.97 CFO and $6.42 FCF after $3.55 CapEx.

web_blocks.caption: Constituent-Level Audited Unit Economics (Per $100 of Company Revenue)
web_blocks.takeaway: Retailers (WMT, COST, TGT) convert $2.09–$4.20 of FCF per $100 of sales via rapid inventory turns, whereas CPG leaders (PG, PEP) convert $8.17–$17.40 per $100 via brand gross margins.

web_blocks.text: 3.3 Working Capital Float and the CapEx Intensity Shift

web_blocks.html: Look at a key cash-conversion feature in the waterfall above: weighted Operating Cash Flow ($9.97 per $100) exceeds weighted Operating Income ($8.98) and Net Income ($7.04). Why? XLP's retail and CPG leaders run on negative working capital. Costco collects cash at the register and upfront annual membership fees ($2.85B deferred fees on its balance sheet) weeks before paying suppliers. It carries $19.78B in accounts payable against $18.12B in inventory. Likewise, Walmart holds $63.06B of accounts payable against $58.85B of inventory, turning stock roughly nine times a year.

At the same time, capital spending has risen structurally. Walmart spent $26.64 billion on CapEx in FY26 (3.74% of sales, up $2.86B YoY) on supply-chain automation and pickup capacity, guiding FY27 CapEx to ~3.5% of sales. P&G spent $4.41 billion (5.07% of FY26 sales) and guides FY27 CapEx to 4.5%–5.5% of sales. Costco spent $5.50 billion expanding its 914-warehouse base. Free cash flow conversion remains strong at $6.42 per $100, but defending omnichannel speed now demands steady reinvestment.

web_blocks.text: 3.4 Sub-Model Unit Economics: Concentrate Incidence, Membership Float & Retail Media

web_blocks.html: Three specialized engines explain why XLP's leaders earn high returns on capital. First, Coca-Cola's incidence-based concentrate pricing ties syrup prices to bottler finished-product sales and mix. KO captures global price/mix upside while keeping bottling CapEx off its books (FY25 CapEx was just $2.1B on $47.9B revenue, or 4.4%). Second, Costco's membership flywheel turns $5.32B of annual fees—which carry almost zero incremental COGS—into over half of its $10.38B operating income. That fee stream subsidizes ~12.8% merchandise gross margins that rivals cannot match.

Third, Walmart's ecosystem layering is lifting retail margins. Core Walmart U.S. stores earn a 5.2% operating margin, yet Walmart's global ad business jumped 46% to nearly $6.4 billion in FY26. Global membership fees also grew 15.1% in Q4 FY26. Because retail media carries software-like margins and reduces cost of sales or lifts net sales, it helps offset last-mile delivery costs. That is how Walmart grew consolidated operating income faster than revenue.

The main supply-chain risk in XLP is commodity and tariff pass-through lag. Input shocks—like cocoa for Mondelez, aluminum for bottlers, or import tariffs for retailers—hit cost of goods sold within one or two quarters. Shelf-price hikes and productivity offsets take two to four quarters to catch up. In FY25, PepsiCo's North America beverage unit absorbed a 6-point commodity cost hit from tariffs (11 points in Q4). Mondelez absorbed a 1,070 bps gross margin drop from cocoa inflation.

On the retail floor, inventory discipline separates winners from laggards. In FY26, Walmart's constant-currency inventory grew 2.6% against 5.1% constant-currency revenue growth, avoiding clearance markdowns. Sam's Club inventory grew only 1.6%. Costco ended FY25 with $18.12B in inventory against $19.78B in payables, so suppliers funded 109% of its warehouse stock. Target ended FY24 with $12.74B in inventory against $13.05B in payables while managing higher discretionary markdown risk.

web_blocks.title: Supply-Chain Audit Check: Payables-to-Inventory Coverage
paragraphs: Across XLP's retail giants, Accounts Payable exceeds Merchandise Inventory (Costco 109%, Walmart 107%, Target 102%).
This supplier-funded working capital float is the structural reason XLP's weighted Operating Cash Flow ($9.97 per $100) exceeds Net Income ($7.04 per $100) even during heavy CapEx cycles.

web_blocks.text: 3.6 Geographic & Channel Mix Impact on Unit Economics

web_blocks.html: Channel & Geographic Mix: Convenience stores and away-from-home venues carry far higher gross margins per ounce than bulk multi-packs for Coca-Cola, PepsiCo, and Altria. When budget-strained shoppers shift from convenience stores to clubs and supercenters, beverage and snack makers face negative channel mix. Meanwhile, Sam's Club U.S. ($93.0B FY26 sales) grew Q4 eCommerce 23% while holding its 11.3% gross margin and 2.6%–2.7% operating margin steady.

Packaging, Freight & Automation Leverage: P&G's FY27 outlook flags ~$1.0 billion in after-tax headwinds from raw materials, energy, and freight. Management plans to offset those costs with productivity savings (460 bps gross productivity in Q4 FY26). In retail, Walmart U.S. grew Q4 eCommerce 27% while leveraging operating expenses by 2 bps—proving that automated fulfillment centers can bend the labor cost curve.

CapEx Intensity vs. Asset-Light Split: Across XLP's core, CapEx intensity varies nearly 3x. Costco (2.00% of FY25 sales) and Target (2.71% of FY24 sales) run lean store CapEx ratios. Walmart (3.74% FY26) and P&G (5.07% FY26) are in heavier modernization cycles. Crucially, every flagship holding funds 100% of CapEx internally from operating cash flow without issuing dilutive equity.

Store-Level Labor & Shrink Controls: Across XLP's 34.75% retail sleeve, store labor and inventory shrink directly govern operating leverage. Walmart U.S. grew Q4 FY26 net sales 4.6% while operating income rose 6.6%, proving store productivity outpaced wage costs. Target also monitors vendor compliance and shrink closely to protect its 5.2% operating margin.

Private-Label Gross Margin Advantage: Store brands like Kirkland Signature and Great Value typically carry higher percentage gross margins for retailers than national brands. That extra margin room lets Costco and Walmart hold sharp shelf prices while funding warehouse wages and digital pickup.

Store-to-Home Fulfillment Economics: Store-fulfilled delivery lets Walmart leverage existing neighborhood store footprints rather than building costly standalone fulfillment warehouses. That model cuts last-mile driving distances and raises inventory turns across its 4,605 U.S. locations.

Supplier Consolidation & Scale Rebates: High-volume retailers use centralized procurement to lock in multi-year supplier terms. Those volume rebates reduce cost of goods sold and fund everyday low pricing for members.
Supply-Chain Resilience: Multi-sourcing across domestic and international plants helps XLP's manufacturers absorb localized port delays or weather disruptions without losing shelf availability.

Warehouse Club Renewal Economics: High annual membership renewal rates keep Costco customer acquisition costs near zero. That recurring fee base stabilizes store-level cash flow across economic cycles.

book_paragraphs: If you want to know whether a sector is truly defensive, follow every hundred dollars of customer sales down to free cash flow. Because XLP is an ETF, it does not publish a consolidated GAAP income statement. So you and I must build a look-through waterfall from the audited annual filings of its core holdings.

First, picture the two physical supply chains running inside XLP. On the brand side, PepsiCo's Frito-Lay and Coca-Cola's bottlers rely on Direct-Store-Delivery. Route trucks bypass central grocery warehouses to stock chips and sodas straight onto end-caps and coolers. That gives brands tight control over display, though it demands heavy driver and fleet spending. On the retail side, Walmart, Costco, and Target run cross-docking warehouses and store-backroom hubs. In Q4 fiscal 2026, Walmart's expedited store-fulfilled delivery surged over 50%, turning 4,605 U.S. supercenters into local eCommerce depots.

Now let us trace the dollars across five audited bellwethers—Walmart, Costco, Procter & Gamble, Target, and PepsiCo—representing nearly 38% of XLP. Weighting their latest full-year filings by XLP weights gives a crisp $100 breakdown. Out of every $100.00 of weighted revenue, $69.32 goes to cost of goods sold, leaving $30.68 of gross profit. Another $19.38 covers operating expenses excluding depreciation, and $2.32 covers depreciation and amortization. That leaves $8.98 of operating income.

After a $0.40 net interest drag, $0.40 of other income, and $1.94 in taxes, the basket earns $7.04 of net income. Now watch the cash flow statement. Because these firms collect cash at checkout while stretching supplier payables, weighted operating cash flow rises to $9.97 per $100 of sales. Subtract $3.55 of capital expenditures, and XLP's core basket produces $6.42 of pure free cash flow on every $100 of revenue.

Beneath that clean average sits a sharp split in how the two halves of XLP make money. Walmart generates $2.09 of free cash flow per $100 of sales, and Costco generates $2.85, because they pass scale savings back to shoppers. Procter & Gamble, by contrast, converts $17.40 of every $100 into free cash flow via its 50.2% brand gross margin. XLP's aggregate free-cash-flow margin is lower than a pure CPG fund, yet far more resilient when shoppers trade down.

The watchpoint on unit economics is rising capital spending. In fiscal 2026, Walmart poured $26.64 billion into CapEx—up nearly $2.9 billion in one year—to automate warehouses and pickup. P&G guides fiscal 2027 CapEx to 4.5% to 5.5% of sales, and Costco spent $5.50 billion on new clubs. Even defensive compounders must reinvest heavily in automation just to hold their edge.

Three specialized models explain why XLP's leaders still earn strong returns on capital. First, Coca-Cola's incidence-based concentrate pricing links syrup prices to bottler sales while keeping bottling CapEx off KO's balance sheet. Second, Costco's $5.32 billion membership fee stream carries almost no incremental cost, funding rock-bottom warehouse prices. Third, Walmart's $6.4 billion advertising business adds software-like margins that subsidize home delivery.

Every supply chain also faces a timing lag when input costs spike. In 2025, surging cocoa prices cut Mondelez's reported gross margin by over ten points to 28.4% before price hikes could catch up. Tariffs hit PepsiCo's North American beverage commodity costs by 6 percentage points for the year and 11 points in Q4. Meanwhile, disciplined inventory management protected retailers: Walmart grew constant-currency inventory just 2.6% against 5.1% sales growth, and Costco's suppliers funded 109% of its inventory.

Channel mix matters just as much. Cold twenty-ounce sodas at convenience stores earn far higher margins per ounce than multi-pack cases at Costco, so shopper trade-downs create mix drag for CPG firms. Yet Sam's Club proved digital convenience can scale cleanly, growing Q4 eCommerce 23% while holding its 11.3% gross margin steady.

Finally, notice how automation is bending the retail labor curve. Skeptics once warned that curbside pickup would crush grocery margins, yet Walmart U.S. grew Q4 eCommerce 27% while leveraging operating expenses by 2 bps. Best of all, every flagship company inside XLP funds 100% of its CapEx from internal operating cash flow without diluting shareholders.

Let us trace a concrete example of working capital float so you can see it in action. Suppose Costco sells a pallet of Kirkland olive oil on Monday morning. The shopper pays by debit card at the register, putting cash in Costco's bank account within forty-eight hours. Costco may not pay the olive-oil supplier for thirty days.

Multiply that thirty-day float across $270 billion of annual sales, and you get a massive interest-free loan from suppliers. That is why Costco holds $19.78 billion in accounts payable against $18.12 billion in inventory. Growth actually generates cash upfront rather than tying it up in warehouses.

Now contrast that with a packaged-food maker like Mondelez. Mondelez must buy cocoa beans, wheat, and sugar months ahead of production, process them in factories, ship them to distributors, and wait weeks for grocers to pay. Its working capital cycle is far slower, which is why its brand gross margin must be much higher to earn a good return on capital.

Look also at how store-level labor and shrink affect the retail side of XLP. In a low-margin business earning four or five cents on the dollar, even a half-point jump in theft or wage costs can hurt profit. Walmart offset those pressures in fiscal 2026 by growing U.S. operating income 6.6% in Q4 on 4.6% comp sales, powered by automation and ad revenue.

Private-label goods also boost retail unit economics. When Walmart sells Great Value pasta or Costco sells Kirkland batteries, they cut out national-brand ad markups. Both chains pocket higher percentage gross margins while still charging shoppers 15% to 25% less than the national brand.

Finally, remember why all of this matters for XLP's cash engine. Whether a constituent earns 3% operating margins on rapid turns or 31% margins on syrup concentrate, every core bellwether in XLP funds its own growth internally. Zero reliance on outside equity dilution keeps per-share cash compounding clean.

Let us look even closer at how eCommerce fulfillment works inside Walmart's 4,605 U.S. stores. Instead of shipping a gallon of milk and a box of cereal from a distant hub via UPS, Walmart picks those items right off local store shelves. Delivery drivers then drop them at nearby doorsteps within two hours.

Using existing stores as fulfillment nodes slashes shipping costs on heavy, low-margin groceries. That is why Walmart's store-fulfilled delivery grew over 50% in Q4 fiscal 2026 while store operating margins expanded.

On the manufacturing side, think about how Procter & Gamble defends its 50.2% gross margin. P&G runs massive automated plants producing Tide, Pampers, and Bounty at global scale. Even small packaging tweaks—like concentrating liquid detergent into smaller bottles—cut plastic, truck weight, and warehouse space all at once.
Those productivity savings matter enormously when freight and resin prices jump. Without continuous plant automation, a 5% spike in raw materials would wipe out years of steady margin gains.

Also keep an eye on Target's $2.89 billion in fiscal 2024 capital spending. Target invests heavily in store remodels and sortation centers to keep Drive Up fast and accurate. Across XLP's retail sleeve, capital efficiency is won in supply-chain software and local store density.

Think about why distribution density is so hard for new entrants to copy. To rival PepsiCo's snack routes or Walmart's regional distribution hubs, a challenger would need tens of billions of dollars in trucks, warehouses, and store relationships.

Even digital-first brands eventually hit that physical wall. Selling heavy bottles of laundry detergent or twelve-packs of soda one box at a time through parcel carriers destroys gross margin. Delivering them on full pallets to Walmart or Costco preserves the economics.
That physical reality is why XLP's incumbent supply chains remain so valuable. Scale logistics turn low-priced daily goods into reliable, multi-billion-dollar cash flow streams.
Look also at how digital loyalty programs tighten the retail flywheel. Programs like Walmart+ and Target Circle link fuel savings and free delivery directly to repeat grocery orders.
Once a family pays for an annual membership, they consolidate more weekly trips at that chain, lifting store turnover and cash conversion.
That internal funding loop—where scale logistics and negative working capital finance store and plant upgrades—is the true heartbeat of XLP's unit economics.
Every dollar of CapEx is earned inside the business first, keeping balance sheets clean while funding modern logistics.

book_callouts.title: NARRATOR'S REFLECTION: Negative Working Capital Is the Hidden Moat
paragraphs: Notice that weighted operating cash flow ($9.97 per $100) is 42% higher than net income ($7.04). Retailers like Costco and Walmart effectively finance their inventory with supplier credit and upfront membership fees, turning growth into a source of cash rather than a drain.
